name: Portugal
governanceModel: EU-aligned adopter running the AI Act through telecoms regulator ANACOM while investing in Portuguese-language models (Amália/EuroLLM), EuroHPC compute and AI-led state reform
debateTopics: ANACOM as Portugal's single AI regulator
Sines data centres, subsea cables and compute
overview:
Portugal's AI posture combines faithful EU alignment with an unusually concrete bet on language sovereignty and infrastructure. Rather than creating a new AI authority, the government designated ANACOM -- the telecoms regulator -- as the national market surveillance authority and single point of contact for the EU AI Act in September 2025, coordinating with sectoral bodies (the data protection authority CNPD, Banco de Portugal, securities regulator CMVM) where AI touches their domains. ANACOM has since begun operationalising the Act, consulting in June 2026 on recommendations for applying the Article 5 prohibitions, and is tasked with building Portugal's AI regulatory sandbox. Strategy is set by the National AI Agenda (Agenda Nacional de Inteligência Artificial, ANIA), approved by the Council of Ministers in December 2025 and published as Resolution 2/2026: more than EUR 400 million to 2030 across 32 initiatives under pillars covering infrastructure and data, talent, adoption, and responsibility and ethics -- part of Minister for State Reform Gonçalo Saraiva Matias's broader push to rebuild public administration around AI.

The distinctive artefact is Amália, Portugal's first national large language model: an open-source model in European Portuguese built on the IST/Unbabel-led EuroLLM-9B base by a consortium including the Instituto de Telecomunicações, Instituto Superior Técnico, Unbabel, NOVA University Lisbon and INESC TEC, funded with EUR 5.5 million from the Recovery and Resilience Plan. Declared 'ready' at Web Summit in November 2025 and publicly launched on 1 July 2026, it is being wired into the gov.pt citizen-services portal and public administration -- a small-model sovereignty play rather than a frontier ambition. On compute, Portugal hosts the EuroHPC petascale system Deucalion at the University of Minho, joined Spain and Türkiye at the end of 2025 as a partner in the BSC AI Factory upgrading MareNostrum 5 for AI workloads, and is courting hyperscale AI data-centre investment at Sines (Start Campus), where Atlantic subsea cables and renewable power are pitched as a comparative advantage.

The wider ecosystem punches above its weight in applied AI: Lisbon and Porto produce internationally significant companies (Unbabel in translation, Feedzai in financial crime, Sword Health in digital physical therapy, Talkdesk in contact-centre AI, Defined.ai in training data), IST's ELLIS unit and INESC institutes anchor research, and hosting Web Summit gives Lisbon an outsized convening role in European tech-policy debate. The gaps are equally clear: no frontier lab, modest domestic capital, a thin dedicated AI-policy think-tank scene, and a sandbox and national enforcement architecture still being stood up as the AI Act's obligations phase in.

currentDirection.summary: Portugal tightens in step with the EU AI Act's phase-in (ANACOM designated as supervisor, Article 5 guidance consulted on, GPAI enforcement live from 2 August 2026), but the national energy is promotional: an EUR 400M+ AI agenda, a state-backed open LLM entering public services, and compute and data-centre investment aimed at making Portugal an attractive AI location within EU rules.

recentDevelopments.text: The EU AI Act's supervision and enforcement powers over general-purpose AI (GPAI) models took effect on 2 August 2026, together with the Act's Article 50 transparency duties -- exercised centrally by the European Commission's AI Office rather than by Portuguese regulators. The same date was the deadline for each member state to have an AI regulatory sandbox; ANACOM is tasked with creating and managing Portugal's sandbox, which was still being stood up around the deadline with its timeline aligned to the high-risk obligations phasing in to 2027.

Amália, Portugal's first national large language model, was officially launched into public deployment on 1 July 2026 -- an open-source model for European Portuguese built on the EuroLLM-9B base by a consortium including the Instituto de Telecomunicações, Instituto Superior Técnico, Unbabel, NOVA University Lisbon and INESC TEC, with EUR 5.5 million from the Recovery and Resilience Plan (PRR). Early deployments include a virtual assistant on the gov.pt public-services portal, with education, culture, media, science and health applications planned.

ANACOM launched a public consultation (16 June - 16 July 2026) on draft recommendations for implementing Article 5 of the AI Act -- the prohibited AI practices, applicable since 2 February 2025 and carrying fines up to EUR 35M or 7% of global turnover -- one of the first substantive acts of national AI Act operationalisation by Portugal's designated supervisor.

The National AI Agenda (Agenda Nacional de Inteligência Artificial, ANIA) was formally published as Council of Ministers Resolution 2/2026 after approval on 4 December 2025, alongside a National Digital Strategy and Digital Skills Pact. ANIA commits more than EUR 400 million to 2030 across 32 initiatives under four pillars -- infrastructure and data, talent, adoption, and responsibility and ethics -- spanning universities, research centres, companies and public administration.

At the end of 2025 the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking signed the contract to expand MareNostrum 5 for AI workloads under the BSC AI Factory -- a EUR 129 million investment in which Portugal is a partner alongside Spain and Türkiye, with participation managed by the Foundation for Science and Technology (FCT), supported by the National Center for Advanced Computing and PRR funding. Installation is scheduled during 2026.

At Web Summit in Lisbon, Minister for State Reform Gonçalo Saraiva Matias announced that the Amália LLM was ready, floated an 'AI tutor per student' ambition for schools, and argued Portugal's Atlantic submarine-cable landings give it a structural advantage in AI -- capping a year in which the government framed AI as the engine of its state-reform programme.

The government designated ANACOM, the national communications regulator, as Portugal's market surveillance authority and single point of contact for the EU AI Act -- choosing to lead AI supervision through an existing regulator that coordinates with sectoral authorities (CNPD for data protection, Banco de Portugal, CMVM) rather than creating a standalone AI agency.

upcomingMilestones.text: Deferred EU AI Act compliance deadline for standalone high-risk (Annex III) AI systems -- postponed from August 2026 by the Digital Omnibus -- the phase most demanding for Portuguese deployers and for ANACOM's market-surveillance and sandbox machinery.

policyAndRegulation.title: EU AI Act (applied via ANACOM as single point of contact)
policyAndRegulation.summary: Portugal has no standalone national AI law; the EU AI Act applies directly, with ANACOM designated in September 2025 as market surveillance authority and single point of contact, coordinating with sectoral regulators (CNPD, Banco de Portugal, CMVM). Prohibited practices have applied since February 2025, GPAI enforcement (via the Commission's AI Office) since 2 August 2026, and most high-risk obligations phase in to August 2027. ANACOM consulted on Article 5 implementation guidance in mid-2026.

policyAndRegulation.title: National AI Agenda (ANIA) -- Council of Ministers Resolution 2/2026
policyAndRegulation.summary: Portugal's main AI policy instrument, approved December 2025 and published January 2026: more than EUR 400 million to 2030 across 32 initiatives under four pillars (infrastructure and data, talent, adoption, responsibility and ethics), aiming to lift productivity, modernise public services and reduce external dependency in compute and data. Sits alongside the National Digital Strategy and Digital Skills Pact within the State Reform agenda.

policyAndRegulation.title: Portuguese Charter of Human Rights in the Digital Age (Law 27/2021)
policyAndRegulation.summary: An early, rights-based digital law that predates the AI Act and includes a provision on the use of AI and robots (requiring respect for fundamental rights and non-discrimination in algorithmic decisions). Largely principles-level, it gives Portuguese courts and regulators a domestic hook for AI-related rights questions.

policyAndRegulation.title: AI regulatory sandbox (ANACOM)
policyAndRegulation.summary: Under the AI Act every member state was to have at least one AI regulatory sandbox operational by 2 August 2026, with priority fee-free access for SMEs and startups. ANACOM is tasked with creating and managing Portugal's sandbox; as of mid-2026 it was not yet operational, with its timeline aligned to the 2027 high-risk phase-in.

researchEcosystem.summary: Portuguese AI research clusters around Lisbon and Porto. Instituto Superior Técnico (IST) and the Instituto de Telecomunicações anchor NLP and machine learning -- including the IST/Unbabel-led EuroLLM open European model family that Amália builds on -- with INESC-ID and the ELLIS Lisbon unit (LUMLIS) alongside; Porto contributes INESC TEC and the University of Porto, and NOVA University Lisbon adds NOVA LINCS. The Champalimaud Foundation is internationally notable in neuroscience-adjacent AI. Compute comes from the EuroHPC petascale system Deucalion at the University of Minho (Guimarães), managed by FCT, plus Portugal's partnership in the BSC AI Factory. The profile is strong applied research and language technology rather than frontier-scale model training.

notableGaps.area: No frontier lab or frontier-scale compute
notableGaps.note: Portugal's model ambitions top out at the 9B-parameter, open-source Amália/EuroLLM scale; there is no domestic frontier developer, and training compute depends on EuroHPC allocations (Deucalion, MareNostrum 5) rather than sovereign GPU capacity -- hence frontierDeveloper 'emerging'.

notableGaps.area: Enforcement architecture still being stood up
notableGaps.note: ANACOM's designation is recent, its Article 5 guidance was only consulted on in mid-2026, the regulatory sandbox missed the notional August 2026 deadline, and no national implementing law with penalties had been enacted -- practical AI Act enforcement capacity remains largely untested.

Portugal lacks specialised AI-governance think tanks; policy debate runs through general foundations, law firms, universities and Web Summit stages rather than dedicated institutes, so several think-tank attributions here carry needsVerification.

Flagship AI companies (Sword Health, Talkdesk) have shifted headquarters or capital bases to the US, and domestic venture funding is modest relative to the ANIA's ambitions -- the recurring worry is that Portugal trains talent and seeds companies whose value accrues elsewhere.

debates.topic: ANACOM as Portugal's single AI regulator
debates.summary: Portugal chose its telecoms regulator as AI Act supervisor and single point of contact -- a pragmatic reuse of an existing institution that raises questions about capacity, independence and coordination with the data protection authority.
debates.expanded: The September 2025 designation made ANACOM market surveillance authority and single point of contact, coordinating with CNPD, Banco de Portugal and CMVM in their domains. Supporters point to ANACOM's regulatory experience and the speed of avoiding a new agency; sceptics ask whether a spectrum-and-telecoms body can build AI supervision expertise fast enough, how fundamental-rights oversight will mesh with CNPD's remit, and why the regulatory sandbox slipped past the AI Act's August 2026 expectation. The mid-2026 Article 5 consultation was ANACOM's first real test of the role.

debates.summary: Portugal built and open-sourced a national LLM for European Portuguese and is deploying it in public services -- a distinctive small-model sovereignty strategy whose payoff is contested.
debates.expanded: Amália -- built on EuroLLM-9B by IT, IST, Unbabel, NOVA and INESC TEC with EUR 5.5M of PRR money -- bets that a modest, open, culturally grounded model wired into gov.pt and public administration is worth more to Portugal than renting frontier capability. Advocates see linguistic dignity (European vs Brazilian Portuguese), public-sector control and a European open-model contribution; critics note 9B parameters is far from the frontier, question uptake against free access to far stronger commercial models, and warn the symbolism could outrun the utility. Its integration into citizen services through 2026-27 is the empirical test.

debates.topic: Sines data centres, subsea cables and compute
debates.summary: Portugal is pitching Atlantic cable landings, renewable power and the Sines campus as its route into the AI infrastructure economy, alongside EuroHPC partnerships.
debates.expanded: The infrastructure pillar of ANIA leans on three assets: the EuroHPC Deucalion machine in Guimarães, partnership in the BSC AI Factory upgrading MareNostrum 5 (contract signed end-2025, installation during 2026), and private hyperscale buildout at Start Campus in Sines, marketed on subsea connectivity and green energy. Boosters -- including Minister Matias at Web Summit -- argue geography gives Portugal a durable niche; sceptics raise grid and water constraints, the gap between hosting data centres and capturing AI value, and dependence on foreign hyperscaler demand for the Sines bet to pay off.

debates.summary: The government has made AI the engine of its state-reform programme -- from licensing processes to an 'AI tutor per student' ambition -- raising both productivity hopes and oversight concerns.
debates.expanded: Minister Gonçalo Saraiva Matias frames AI as the way to rebuild Portuguese public administration: automating licensing, deploying Amália as a citizen-services assistant on gov.pt, a Digital Skills Pact, and floated AI tutors in schools. The promise is a leaner, faster state in a country long frustrated by bureaucracy; the debate concerns realism of the EUR 400M+ envelope against the ambition, safeguards when algorithmic systems touch citizens' rights (where the Charter of Human Rights in the Digital Age and CNPD apply), and whether adoption targets will survive Portugal's political and budget cycles.
